items.article: Georgina Le Grice is no stranger to horror stories, but she never expected to find herself in one when her family's picturesque 18th-century property was falling apart, and there was no money to save it. Georgina Le Grice is no stranger to horror stories, thanks to her job as a London-based literary agent. But she never expected to find herself in one, at her family’s Cornish mansion, Trereife House. The picturesque 18th-century property was falling apart, and there was no money to save it. ‘I moved into Trereife House when I was just two,’ says Georgina, 24, ‘and my elderly grandmother moved out. It had 80 acres of land, 14 rooms and six enormous, ornate bedrooms. We never had heating, and I went to bed in winter in layers of clothes and with two duvets. But I didn’t mind, because I loved the house.’ From a young age, Georgina knew she and her younger brother Peter, 23, were heirs to an estate with a remarkable history. The house has been home to the Le Grice family since 1798. Saviour: Ruth Watson at Trereife House in Penzance with Tim, Peter, Georgina and Elizabeth Le Grice But generation after generation was hit by crippling death duties and running costs. In 1982, it was inherited by Georgina’s father Tim, who runs a law firm. He moved his wife, Liz, and their two children in a few years later.

items.article: A top recruiter has issued a warning to Australians. Published: 04:16, 1 October 2026 | Updated: 04:36, 1 October 2026 Australians are facing a 'dismal' job market, with fierce competition as a result of immigration, an overreliance on university degrees and a lack of vacancies, a recruitment expert warns. According to the latest Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data, the unemployment rate rose from 4.5 per cent in July to 4.6 per cent in August, the highest level recorded since the Covid pandemic. The number of unemployed Australians also increased by 28,200 to 722,900 over the same period. Top recruiter Tammie Ballis, who runs Realistic Careers in Sydney, said she believed that 'too much immigration too quickly' contributed to the influx of applicants chasing the same roles. 'We have seen too many people enter the job market in a short amount of time, and it is unfair to both immigrants and Australians,' she told the Daily Mail on Thursday.

TURNING up the heating will not make a home feel properly cosy if warm air is escaping through gaps and cold air is slipping back in. Draughts often come from overlooked spots rather than one obvious hole, so a chilly room can stay uncomfortable even while the boiler works harder. James Bryant, Founder of made-to-measure interiors specialists Cut My , said: “On a cold or windy day, use the back of your hand to check around windows, doors, floor edges and unused fireplaces. items.article: Although the main aim for most is to improve their health, the potential impact on our bank accounts is also highly appealing. Today marks the beginning of Stoptober and Sober October – the popular month-long challenges which see Britons quit smoking tobacco and drinking alcohol. But how much money does completing 31 days of sobriety and tobacco abstinence actually save – and where's the best place to stash the cash? Britons spend around £15.60 on alcoholic drinks in a week – slightly more than half of which is drunk at home, Office for National Statistics data shows. Smokers fork out an average of £63.91 a week on cigarettes. The average smoker has 11 a day while a cigarette costs 83p each on average. If you take the challenge and stick with it, you could save a small fortune, experts say It means you could save hundreds of pounds if you manage to give up smoking or drinking this October.

items.key: ai:i got a first look at apple's new £2k iphone – it's not just the price that makes it stand out
items.text: I got a first look at Apple’s new £2k iPhone – it’s not just the price that makes it stand out
items.article: After years of holding out, Apple has learnt from its rivals with its first folding model, the iPhone Duo. These are my first impressions The products or services listed have been independently tested by our journalists. We earn a commission from the affiliate links in this article. Read more > Apple has entered the foldable phone race with the iPhone Duo, following years of speculation about whether the company would ever bend its famously rigid design philosophy. Barely a month after Samsung dropped its latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 , this is the moment Apple stakes its claim in a category it has avoided for the last decade. I was at the launch event at Apple’s HQ in Cupertino, California for a first look. Similar in size to a British passport, the new smartphone unfolds like a miniature book to reveal a large 7.6-inch inner screen. When closed, it’s shorter and wider than a traditional iPhone, and when opened, it resembles a small iPad. What makes the iPhone Duo worth your attention isn’t just that it’s the first hinged phone with an Apple logo, but that it addresses some of the biggest frustrations currently plaguing folding mobiles. You can barely see the crease on the inner display, and it doesn’t look like a cheap plastic sheet. It’s intuitive to use, and fully waterproof, which is rare among rivals. Whether all that justifies a £2,000 price tag, however, is another question entirely.

items.key: ai:how to tell if someone is lying to you, according to a psychologist - and why avoiding your gaze does not mean they're bluffing
items.text: How to tell if someone is lying to you, according to a psychologist - and why avoiding your gaze does NOT mean they're bluffing
items.article: If you think you can spot a liar from a mile away, you're probably getting it wrong. By XANTHA LEATHAM, EXECUTIVE SCIENCE EDITOR Published: 10:06, 20 September 2026 | Updated: 10:06, 20 September 2026 A psychologist has revealed that many of the classic signs we associate with lying – for example a shifty glance or nervous fidget – could be completely innocent. Dr Sasha Hall, a Senior Educational Psychologist working with Live Casinos , says people are often far too quick to treat individual behaviours as evidence that someone is bluffing. 'People often rely on popular ideas about body language, such as avoiding eye contact or fidgeting, but these behaviours can occur for many different reasons,' she said. 'Someone might be tired, anxious, distracted or simply thinking carefully about their answer.'
